answer.rationale: The 90-minute latency climb on the write path began roughly 30 minutes after a release went out 2 hours ago, and the degradation is confined to the primary region. Memory b1 documents that rolling back a release cleared a checkout error spike with the prior build stable and no customer impact. Memory b6 confirms that staged release gating and canary cohorts are effective at catching regressions quickly, which supports the hypothesis that this release is the causal factor. With settlement traffic at daily peak, writes are heavy and latency at 5x target threatens write-path availability; rolling back restores the known-stable prior build fastest, preserving all in-flight writes while eliminating the suspected regression. Regional failover (memory b2) would also restore latency but is a heavier operation and the signal here points more strongly at a release regression than a region-level fault. Adding capacity or routing reads to replicas would not address a write-path regression. Circuit breakers are not indicated because no external dependency failure is described. Verification budget is spent confirming the rollback playbook (b1) and the release-gating precedent (b6).
